newsitem.title: KAZAKHSTAN: FOCUS - Kazakh bond issue to mop up pension arrears.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Kazakh bond issue to mop up pension arrears.

text.p: Oil-rich Kazakhstan, under pressure to clear a mountain of pension arrears, on Tuesday announced a $250-350 million Eurobond issue for September or October, and the market reaction was positive.

"There should be a lot of interest," said Eric Fine, head of Russia and East Europe research at banker Morgan Stanley in London. The market snapped up Kazakhstan's debut $200 million, three-year Eurobond last December.
"This is a better bond as its longer duration gives a more positive view of Kazakh credit," Fine said.

Announcing the new plan, Daniyar Abulgazin, chief of treasury at the former Soviet republic's finance ministry, told Reuters: "In September or October, Kazakhstan will issue dollar denominated Eurobonds for a total of $250-350 million."
"The maturity is likely to be five or seven years with concrete terms to be established in line with market conditions," he said.
The finance ministry said it had chosen U.S. investment bank JP Morgan Ltd to lead manage the new issue and, more importantly for the proud Kazakhs, to negotiate a higher credit rating.
Moody's Investors Service last year assigned Kazakhstan a Ba3 sovereign rating for long-term foreign currency bonds while Standard and Poor's rated the republic BB minus.

Kazakhstan, which has nearly finished privatising its strategic oil and gas industry in a fire-sale of state assets unprecedented for a former Soviet republic, was disappointed to achieve a rating lower than neighbouring Russia's.

But Kazakhstan's oil and gas riches are imprisoned in a web of Soviet-built export pipelines controlled by its old colonial master, Russia, which makes available only limited capacity for Kazakh crude.

The Kazakh capital Almaty, jammed at the foot of the towering Tien Shan mountain range, exudes a boom atmosphere and has attracted more than $3 billion in foreign investment with promises of a further $40 billion.
But oil transport hangs heavy over the economic future of this landlocked country five times the size of France.
Kazakh Prime Minister Akezhan Kazhelgeldin faces the sack if he fails to meet President Nursultan Nazarbayev's year-end deadline to pay off 36 billion tenge ($480 million) in pension arrears.
International finance sources in Almaty say Kazhegeldin, through the bond issue and bonuses reaped from oil privatisations, will be able to find the cash without stoking inflation.
Inflation is targeted at about 17 percent while the republic achieved modest GDP growth of 1.1 percent last year in a turnaround from Kazakhstan's post-idependence economic collapse in 1991.
